today.h: The AI Funding Bill: an Eighth Straight Chip Slide, a $110 Barrel — and Six Sectors Held Green
today.c1: The funding question: chips fell for an eighth straight session — the longest slide since 2008 — and the Nasdaq tumbled 2.14% to 26,140.03, its first weekly loss in five weeks and its worst week since June (-4.5%). The S&P 500 fell 1.09% to 7,659.44; the Dow only 0.34% to 52,002.41. The trigger: CoreWeave sank 12% (its bond yields above 15%, levels that typically signal distress) and Reuters reported some Anthropic IPO investors weighing a lower valuation. The split: six of 11 sectors closed green — energy +2.5% best, utilities +1.3%, staples +1.1% — as Brent settled $109.86 (+3.7%, its first $110 touch since May) and WTI $101.41 (+3.5%, highest since Sept 17); the VIX jumped 21% to 19.99. The cushion: Warsh offered no signal at the IMF in Bangkok — October hike odds fell to ~17% (from 28%) — the dollar slipped 0.2%, and Europe closed higher (Stoxx 600 +0.72%, its strongest week since late June). The anomalies: Tesla -2.1% as its Roadster pop faded; Apple +0.5%, the only Magnificent Seven name green; Strategy -10% after MSCI moved to exclude digital-asset treasuries. Next: earnings season, and the Fed's Oct 27-28 meeting.
today.c4:
• The financing file is the swing factor: CoreWeave's bond yields above 15% and Anthropic's IPO repricing are the market's newest price signals — watch them before the tape.
  • The rotation is the cushion: six sectors green, the Dow down only 0.34%, energy leading on the barrel — if breadth keeps absorbing the AI complex's cuts, the scare stays contained.
  • Next week's gates: earnings season, housing and claims data, then the Fed's Oct 27-28 meeting — October odds at ~17% say no shock is expected; December (~89%) is where the risk sits.

chains.t: ① The AI Complex's Third Leg: an Eighth Straight Chip Slide
steps: The rollover: after Wednesday's CPI shock and Thursday's bounce, the AI complex sold off again — CoreWeave -12%, its bonds above 15% (distress territory), and chipmakers fell for an eighth straight session, the longest slide since 2008

The bill: the damage was financing-shaped — hyperscalers veering toward $1 trillion of annual capex, much of it debt-funded (Bloomberg Intelligence); some Anthropic IPO investors weighing a lower valuation after a financial disclosure (Reuters)
The mechanics: semis led — SOXX -4% (8% this week through Thursday), the memory ETF DRAM -5.5%; Micron -5.6%, AMD -6%, Broadcom -4.5%, Intel -5.8%; neocloud peers Nebius and IREN slid over 3% early
The scoreboard: Nasdaq -2.14% to 26,140.03 — its worst week since June; S&P -1.09% to 7,659.44; VIX +21% to 19.99 — and all but seven of the tech sector's 75 stocks closed lower
The counter-voices: Cathie Wood's ARK added CoreWeave and Cerebras into the decline ('investing in the AI computing supplier will pay off'); the debate is now about financing, not demand
chains.d: The main chain: this week's AI-complex selling was financing-shaped — distress-level bond yields, a trillion-dollar capex bill and an IPO repricing — and it capped the Nasdaq's worst week since June while the rest of the market held.

news.fact: Another burst of selling in technology shares drove the Nasdaq 100 to its worst week since the April 2025 tariff turmoil as investors questioned the outlook for the artificial-intelligence trade. Chipmakers fell for an eighth straight day, the longest slide since 2008. CoreWeave Inc., a cloud-computing services provider whose bonds recently hit levels that typically signal distress, sank 12%. The S&P 500 lost 1.1%.

The biggest tech companies, known as hyperscalers, are veering toward $1 trillion of annual capital spending, according to Bloomberg Intelligence. Much of that is debt funded. While tech giants mostly have high-grade credit ratings, fund managers are asking more questions about junk-rated borrowers like CoreWeave.

CoreWeave shares finished down 12%, a second big drop in three days. They had fallen more than 15% earlier in the week on concerns about the Nvidia-backed firm's debt before rising 6% yesterday. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS) declined 2%, with Meta Platforms down nearly 4%. Nvidia, the world's most valuable public company, was 1.5% lower. Apple, which finished up about 0.5%, was the only member of the septet in the green.
Nvidia-backed CoreWeave slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data center operator's bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%.

Some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming initial public offering are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures, four people familiar with the matter said. Some investors discussed a valuation of around $1.5 trillion, a significant step down from the roughly $2 trillion that investors had previously expected for the November share sale.

Micron Technology fell 5.6%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6%, Broadcom lost 4.5% and Intel gave up 5.8%. Investors are now worried that the companies, which have relied on debt markets to finance an investment spree into their technology, may not be able to keep borrowing and spending as heavily with yields in bond markets worldwide recently climbing to their highest levels in years.

Other stocks connected to the AI trade fell after pulling back yesterday. Roundhill's Memory ETF (DRAM), which had already logged a double-digit retreat over the week's first four sessions, sank 5.5% further, pulled lower by components Western Digital, Sandisk, Micron Technology and Seagate Technology. The broader iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was 4% lower after having fallen 8% this week through Thursday.

Concerns over CoreWeave's high borrowing costs are common for young companies raising money when rates are elevated, but investing in the AI computing supplier will pay off, noted Cathie Wood of ARK Investment Management LLC. She compared CoreWeave to Coinbase. ARK Investment added both CoreWeave and Cerebras Systems Inc. during this week's declines, Wood said.

chains.t: ② The Barrel: Brent's First $110 Since May — the Diesel Deal Meets a War Weekend
steps: The morning fade: crude slid early as traders weighed how much diesel Russia can actually deliver — then reversed hard as 'escalation fears resurfaced amid rumours of attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure' (Energy Aspects)

The war leg: a ballistic missile toward Yanbu was intercepted; Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia continued; Ukraine hit Russia's Ryazan refinery after Zelenskiy dropped the energy-site ceasefire; Eurasia Group raised escalation odds to 65% from 35%
The settles: Brent +3.7% to $109.86 — a first $110 touch since May, highest since May 19; WTI +3.5% to $101.41, highest since Sept 17; the week: Brent +4.9%, WTI +10.4%

The squeeze: diesel settled $4.90 a gallon in New York — highest-ever seasonally, with European diesel futures up more than twofold this year; the US offered up to 17 million barrels from the SPR; the IEA agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of fuel
The counter-move: House lawmakers introduced the Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act to block the diesel deal; the equity echo — energy +2.5%, best sector, Exxon +2.5%, Chevron +2.6%
chains.d: The barrel: a deal meant to flood the market with Russian diesel met a war that keeps taking supply off it — Brent's first $110 since May, the week's best sector, and a product squeeze at record seasonal prices.

news.fact: Brent touched $110 a barrel for the first time since May on worries that escalating tensions in the Middle East could further tighten supplies, while investors assessed how much diesel Russia could supply to the global market. Brent crude futures settled $3.94, or 3.7%, higher at $109.86, the highest since May 19, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures closed $3.44, or 3.5%, higher at $101.41, the highest since September 17. So far this week, Brent has risen 4.9% and WTI 10.4%.

'WTI and Brent reversed earlier losses as escalation fears resurfaced amid rumours of attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure,' research and consultancy Energy Aspects said in a note. A Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards the Red Sea city of Yanbu. Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites; Russia's Ryazan oil refinery has suspended operations at a primary crude distillation unit following a drone attack.

Brent oil hit $110/bbl for the first time since May as prospects for imminent supply relief dwindle, prompting traders to ramp up bets on higher prices ahead of the weekend. Diesel settled at $4.90 a gallon in New York. Contracts for both commodities are trading at the highest-ever levels seasonally. U.S. lawmakers introduced a bill Friday to block Trump's deal with Moscow to release several hundred million barrels of diesel.

'The conflict is likely to escalate,' Eurasia Group analysts wrote in a note, raising their odds of intensification to 65% from 35%. On Friday, the U.S. offered up to 17 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the Department of Energy said.

A group of House Democrats and one Republican representative introduced a bill to block President Trump's deal to purchase and import Russian diesel, according to a statement from Rep. Gregory Meeks' office. The bill would prohibit the US International Development Finance Corporation from investing in Russian energy, nullify licenses issued by the Office of Foreign Assets Control and ban future licenses, and mandate sanctions on Russian energy.

Brent crude futures settled at $109.86 a barrel, while front-month WTI climbed above $100 for the first time since September. Crude oil prices surged Friday as attacks on commercial vessels around the strait intensified and traders assessed the possibility of further military escalation between Washington and Tehran.
'After a brief reprieve, the oil market is having to price risk back in, particularly heading into the weekend,' said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC Private Wealth Group.

'Conflict in the Middle East still keeps coming back and I think it's questionable how much diesel fuel Russia can actually deliver to the markets. Those two factors are just continuing to have traders be buyers,' said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial.

Forecasters at Goldman Sachs expect oil prices to fall gradually in 2027 but stay above their February 2026 levels, according to a research note released Friday. High prices for crude oil and, in turn, the gasoline and diesel it's turned into have chewed through household budgets.

chains.t: ③ The Cushion: Warsh Stood Down, the Dollar Slipped — and Six Sectors Held Green
steps: The Fed stood down: Warsh offered no fresh signals at the IMF meetings in Bangkok ('It's a new chapter at the Fed, and we're not in that business anymore') — October hike odds fell to ~17% from 28%; December held ~89%
The dollar kept sliding: DXY -0.2% to ~101.8 — euro +0.2% to $1.1239; pound +0.4% to $1.3329; the yen little changed at 157.99
The breadth: six of 11 sectors closed green — energy, utilities, staples, materials, financials, real estate; only slightly more than half of S&P 500 stocks fell; the Dow -0.34% vs the Nasdaq -2.14%

The winners: Alcoa +2.5% and Travelers +1.5% on beats; the market absorbed hot import prices (+1.1% m/m, +8.1% y/y — the largest annual rise since July 2022) and solid industrial production (+0.7%) without re-arming the rate trade
The global close: Europe finished higher — Stoxx 600 +0.72%, its strongest week since late June; DAX +0.95%, CAC +0.28%, FTSE +0.38% — as stronger earnings offset tech-valuation worries
chains.d: The cushion: the Fed's silence, a softer dollar and a broad defensive bid absorbed the tech damage — six sectors held green and the Dow barely moved.

news.fact: The Fed is under pressure to rein in inflation following hotter-than-anticipated CPI and PPI readings this week. Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking at an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok, did not signal how the central bank might act on interest rates at its policy meetings later this month or in early December. 'It's a new chapter at the Fed, and we're not in that business anymore,' Warsh said. Traders now see a 17% likelihood the Fed will raise rates at its late-October meeting, down from 28% yesterday, according to CME FedWatch. They see an 89% likelihood of a rate hike at its December meeting, unchanged from yesterday.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the US economy remained resilient and was benefiting from an AI-driven investment boom. He, however, noted the spending surge was boosting inflation. Markets increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates unchanged this month.
The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index fell 0.2%. The euro rose 0.2% to $1.1239. The British pound rose 0.4% to $1.3329. The Japanese yen was little changed at 157.99 per dollar.

Slightly more than half of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell, but all but seven of the 75 stocks in the index's tech sector closed lower. Among the biggest decliners were chip companies, reflecting mounting worries about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last.
Alcoa rose 2.5% and The Travelers Cos. gained 1.5% after the companies reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street forecasts.

U.S. import prices rose 1.1% in September and 8.1% from a year earlier, the largest annual increase since July 2022. Export prices rose 2.2% on the month. September industrial production increased 0.7%, above expectations, while manufacturing output gained 0.3%.

European equities closed higher, outperforming Wall Street as stronger corporate earnings helped offset concerns about technology valuations and rising financing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600 gained 0.72% to 644.74, completing its strongest weekly advance since late June. Germany's DAX climbed 0.95% to 25,622.61, France's CAC 40 advanced 0.28% to 7,956.70 and the U.K. FTSE 100 rose 0.38% to 10,881.90.

chains.t: ④ The Cross-Currents: Tesla's Roadster Pop Fades, Apple Holds — and Crypto's Index Problem
steps: The Roadster day: Tesla unveiled the SpaceX-thruster Roadster (0-60 in under a second; production 2028) — the stock jumped 4.4% premarket, then faded to -2.1% as the tape rolled over
The merger chatter: Barclays said an all-stock SpaceX-Tesla deal is 'widely viewed as more likely' after the event; SpaceX (SPCX) shares rose 2.1% early
Apple's green print: +0.5% — the only Magnificent Seven name higher — as folding-phone preorders slipped into January within minutes of opening ($1,999; Oct 23 release)

Crypto's index problem: Strategy sank ~10% after MSCI adopted rules to exclude digital-asset treasuries at its November review ('billions of dollars in stock sales' at risk); bitcoin -0.5% to ~$81.6k; ether -1.6%
The rest: Netflix -2.9% as Peter Rice replaced its chief content officer, days after the company said it would cut about 6% of staff (nearly 1,000 roles)
chains.d: The day's cross-currents: a headline pop that faded, the one mega-cap that held, and an index rule that bit the crypto trade — none of it changed the AI verdict.

news.fact: Shares in Tesla fell 2.1% after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new model of its Roadster sports car that can thrust itself up in the air.

Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster on Thursday evening which used SpaceX rocket technology to jump off a ramp and perform a controlled landing. CEO Elon Musk said production of the long-awaited vehicle was set to begin in 2028. The vehicle was able to jump a ramp at a full inversion before using its air thrusters to correct its orientation and land on all four wheels.

The possibility of a merger between Tesla and SpaceX has been raised before — by investors, Street analysts, and even Musk himself — but the arrival of the Roadster prototype has revived the conversation. Barclays flagged overlapping products such as Tesla's Optimus robots and robotaxis using SpaceX's AI, plus the Roadster; SpaceX would benefit from Tesla's free cash flow.

Shipping estimates for Apple Inc.'s first folding phone slipped into January within minutes of the company taking preorders on Friday, suggesting that strong demand and short supply will make the $1,999 device challenging to purchase on its Oct. 23 release date or in the near future.

Shares of Strategy slipped nearly 10% on Friday, in part because bitcoin prices were down, but also because index provider MSCI announced that it would start implementing a prior proposal to make non-operating companies 'ineligible for inclusion' — publicly traded digital asset treasuries listed on its indexes would be shown the door at its November index review.

MSCI Inc. adopted new rules that could ultimately push Strategy Inc. out of its global equity benchmarks, potentially triggering billions of dollars in stock sales and adding fresh pressure to the financing model behind Michael Saylor's vast Bitcoin holdings. Bitcoin fell 0.5% to $81,562.09. Ether fell 1.6% to $2,411.54.

Netflix's stock fell 2.9% a day after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about 6% of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions.

mtd.h: October, Twelve Sessions In: a Record, Three Repricings — and the Gains Handed Back
mtd.d: S&P 7,651.5 to 7,659.44 (+0.10% MTD): twelve sessions delivered one S&P record close, a 24-year ceiling re-tested — and three repricings (wireless 10/9; the AI complex 10/12-13 and again into month-end; the inflation prints 10/14-15). Six sectors still hold gains; the month nets to a round trip.
mtd.c1: Twelve sessions into October and the month nets to a round trip: the S&P is +0.10% MTD at 7,659.44 — its lone record close (7,818.93 on 10/6, its first above 7,800) all but handed back — the Nasdaq -2.68%, the Dow +2.15%. The arc: a 10Y that touched a 24-year high of 5.36% on 10/7 and closed the window at 5.09% (-20bp); three repricings — wireless (10/9), the AI complex (10/12-13, and again into month-end), the inflation prints (10/14-15) — whose October odds round-tripped from 22% before CPI to a 37% peak and back to ~17%; and a barrel that broke out: Brent +12.1% on the December basis, past the $100-107 stretch of the first two weeks. Beneath: Energy (+11.0%), Staples (+8.7%) and Utilities (+7.0%) lead sectors while Tech (-6.3%) sits at the bottom. Gate: the Oct 27-28 meeting.
mtd.c4:
• October's verdict so far: the records came early, three repricings followed — and the AI complex keeps paying the month's rent; the month's engine (AI, deals) still runs while the rate axis charges it.
  • The dispersion signature holds: the barrel's beneficiaries and defensives lead; the AI complex's crowded corners get taxed — the spread between the month's best and worst sectors is ~17 points.
  • The month's referee is still the Fed: October hike odds round-tripped from 22% before CPI to a 37% peak and back to ~17% — the prints fully faded; the Oct 27-28 meeting decides whether the repricing gets another round.

chains.t: ① Twelve Sessions, One Arc: the Record, the Ceiling — and the Repricings
steps: Where the month opened: two Nasdaq records (10/5-6) and one for the S&P (7,818.93 on 10/6, its first above 7,800) — against a 10Y pushing toward 24-year highs
Mid-month: the ceiling re-tested — a 24-year high of 5.36% printed on 10/7 — and auction buyers met each re-test
The repricings: wireless (10/9); the AI complex (10/12-13); the inflation prints (10/14-15) — hot data that moved October hike odds from 22% before CPI to a 37% peak, then fully back to ~17%
The flows: the third repricing's worst beat met rotation money — bonds bid; the 10Y exits the window at 5.09% (-20bp)
The month's math: S&P +0.10%, Nasdaq -2.68%, Dow +2.15% — dispersion over direction
chains.d: Twelve sessions in: the records came early, the ceiling got re-tested, and three repricings followed — the latest met by buyers in part. October's engine runs on; the rate axis charges the rent.

news.fact: Traders now see a 17% likelihood the Fed will raise rates at its late-October meeting, down from 28% yesterday, according to CME FedWatch. They see an 89% likelihood of a rate hike at its December meeting, unchanged from yesterday.

According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 37% likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks, up from 22% before the reading, and a 91% likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting, up from 88% before the data.

Stocks surged Friday, pushing the major indexes to weekly gains, as tech shares rebounded from the previous session's sell-off. The 10-year Treasury yield ended the week around 5.24%, two days after it briefly neared 5.37%, its highest level in more than 24 years.

chains.t: ② The Month's Split: the Barrel's Beneficiaries Lead — the AI Complex Pays
steps: Sector map: Energy (+11.0%), Staples (+8.7%) and Utilities (+7.0%) lead; Tech (-6.3%) sits last
Breadth check: Goldman's dotcom-era warning (10/9) still reads stale — the Dow +2.15% vs the Nasdaq -2.68% MTD, defensives and energy leading
Where the damage landed: memory, equipment and neocloud names led nearly every down-leg of the month
The rotation: ConsDisc +3.3%, Staples +8.7% MTD vs Tech -6.3% — flows left the AI complex without leaving equities
The spread between the month's best and worst sectors: ~17 points — dispersion, not direction
chains.d: October's pattern: the barrel's beneficiaries and defensives collect; each repricing re-cuts the AI complex's crowded corners.

news.fact: Shares of the country's largest telecommunications giants are slumping amid worries about growing competition from SpaceX.

Memory makers Micron and SK Hynix saw their stocks fall after Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) announced significant progress on a new memory-cell design aimed at increasing storage density; CXMT aims to introduce a new server memory product built on the architecture by the end of 2026.
The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index dropped 4.3%, down for a sixth straight session, its longest losing streak since May 2025.

chains.t: ③ The Barrel, Three Weeks In: $100 Held — Then $110
steps: The bid stack: attack counts, strike-risk headlines and shut-ins kept re-arming the war premium — crude held above $100 into the month's final stretch
Policy answered twice: the IEA's accelerated release — and the Russia diesel deal, which now faces legislation to block it
FT's count: 24 ships hit in the two weeks to 10/11 — the war's heaviest stretch of attacks
The scoreboard: Brent $109.86 (+12.1% MTD, Dec basis); WTI $101.41 (+12.2%)
The band broke: October settles ran $100.20-$106.65 through mid-month — then the month's escalation carried the premium past $109
chains.d: October's barrel: supply shocks met policy supply — a $100-107 band, bought on both sides, until it broke upward.

news.fact: Approximately 62.9% of daily offshore oil production, or 1.28 million barrels per day, has been shut in as Hurricane Isaias strengthens ahead of an expected landfall.

Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began — cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October; of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers and two others were crude oil tankers.
'Constraints on the diesel market will extend well into next year,' the International Energy Agency warned, with gasoil supply falling short of demand in 4Q26.

Brent crude settled down 14 cents, or 0.13%, at $105.92 a barrel; US West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled up $2.88, or 3.03%, to $97.97, after a large US crude stock draw helped support prices.

qtd.h: Q4, Twelve Sessions In: +0.10% — a Record, a Ceiling, and the Reckonings
qtd.d: From 9/30's 7,651.5 to 7,659.44 (+0.10% QTD): the opening ledger — one all-time mark, a 24-year top, three repricings, one breakout; the gates still ahead.
qtd.c1: Q4's ledger: +0.10% (7,659.44) for the S&P, -2.68% for the Nasdaq, +2.15% for the Dow. Inside it: one all-time mark set (10/6, first time beyond 7,800); a 24-year top on 10/7 (5.36%) before the long end retreated to 5.09% (-20bp QTD); three repricings booked — telecom names, the AI complex, the CPI-PPI pair — with October hike odds swinging 22% → 37% → ~17%. The $100-107 corridor ended upward (Brent +12.1%, December basis); gold -0.1%; the dollar +0.3%. The character: dispersion — Energy +11.0% QTD against Tech -6.3%. Still ahead: Oct 27-28, October PCE (Oct 29), earnings, the Nov 3 midterms.
qtd.c4:
• The quarter's opening lesson: two hot prints moved October hike odds from 22% before CPI to a 37% peak and back to ~17% — fully faded; the Fed's reaction function is now the whole game.
  • The winners so far: energy and safety plays; the losers: the AI complex's crowded corners — then rescued partly.
  • Duration still sets the terms: the 10Y caps multiples, but its retreat to 5.09% enabled the rotation — a quiet bond market is the bull case's first draft.

chains.t: ① The Q4 Handoff — First Three Weeks
steps: The handoff: 9/30 finished at 7,651.5; it ends at 7,659.44 — the span still holds one S&P all-time mark (7,818.93, 10/6)
The top end: the 10Y posted a 24-year intraday high of 5.36% on 10/7 — demand held each test, then the levels slid
What held it together: a live deal tape, AI compounding — and a revenue scare handled within a session
Then the re-pricings, one per week: telecom names (10/9); the AI complex (10/12-13); the CPI-PPI pair (10/14-15)
And the floor gave: the long end exits at 5.09% (-20bp QTD), under a level held for two weeks
chains.d: Q4's first twelve sessions: a record close, a ceiling re-tested, a scare answered — then three repricings, the latest met by buyers in part.

news.fact: Stocks surged Friday, pushing the major indexes to weekly gains, as tech shares rebounded from the previous session's sell-off. The 10-year Treasury yield ended the week around 5.24%, two days after it briefly neared 5.37%, its highest level in more than 24 years.
According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 29% likelihood the Fed will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks and an 88% likelihood for December.

chains.t: ② The Opening Split: Energy Led — the High-Multiple End Lagged
steps: Leaders: Energy (+11.0%), Staples (+8.7%), Utilities (+7.0%) — the hot-print trade's winners
Laggards: Tech (-6.3%) trails the pack; Comms (-0.6%) pays for the telecom repricing
Small caps: the Russell 2000 at 2,721, after a mid-quarter correction
Inside tech: megacaps held while memory, equipment and neocloud names repriced — before the CPI-PPI pair hit the whole complex
What defines it: dispersion, not a shared tape — the two ends never moved together
chains.d: The quarter's split: energy and defensives got paid; the AI complex's crowded corners paid the tax.

news.fact: Shares of the country's largest telecommunications giants are slumping amid worries about growing competition from SpaceX.
Front Month ICE Brent Crude for Dec. delivery gained $2.47 per barrel, or 2.42% to $104.72 this week — up for two consecutive sessions.

chains.t: ③ The Energy Ledger: Geopolitics vs Policy Offsets — Then a Breakout
steps: Threat re-armed: the conflict's biggest strike week, and Hormuz warnings — tanker traffic at a two-month low
The official answer: the IEA's accelerated release — and a diesel deal now facing a blocking bill
For two weeks both sides traded a $100-107 corridor — every settle from 10/1 to 10/15 inside $100.20-$106.65
Then the corridor cracked: Brent ran to $109.86 — a first $110 touch since May
The final marks: Brent $109.86 (+12.1% QTD, Dec basis); WTI $101.41 (+12.2%)
chains.d: The quarter's oil: price shocks vs policy offsets — a $100-107 corridor that cracked upward as the month escalated.

news.fact: Approximately 62.9% of daily offshore oil production, or 1.28 million barrels per day, has been shut in as Hurricane Isaias strengthens.
President Trump said that Russia will provide diesel supplies to the US and the global marketplace, in a push to bring down the price of refined fuels.

ytd.h: The Bull Meets the Referee: S&P +11.89% as the 10Y's +93bp Sets the Terms
ytd.d: S&P +11.89%, Nasdaq +12.47%, Dow +8.20% with twelve sessions of Q4 logged — AI and earnings carry; the 10Y's +93bp, a hot CPI-PPI pair and an eighth month of war tax the rest.
ytd.c1: The year's base case holds — with the same referee: the bull runs on AI capex and earnings, fighting two taxes — a 10Y up 93bp to 5.09% (fresh 24-year highs printed this month) and oil up ~77% as the war grinds through its eighth month — plus the year's newest twist: hot September prints (CPI 3.7%, PPI 6.3%) whose October hike odds round-tripped 22% → 37% → ~17%. The scoreboard: S&P +11.89%, Nasdaq +12.47%, Dow +8.20%; underneath, Energy (+52.6%) leads the year while Comms (-6.3%) and Consumer Discretionary (-5.8%) lag, and Utilities (-1.1%) slips below water. Nvidia +14.8% YTD as the AI complex's repricings (memory, equipment, credit) cut both ways; gold -3.7% as real rates, not war, dominated; December odds ~89%.
ytd.c4:
• The year's lesson holds: buy where earnings compound (AI infrastructure), rent where rates rule — and the credit file is the newest rent collector.
  • Rates: the 10Y's +93bp is 2026's biggest tax — its October retreat is the bull's best friend; a confirmed Fed pause remains the largest single bullish catalyst left.
  • The bull turned four (10/12) with the AI trade's fault lines visible: power, credit, competition — and now rate sensitivity.

chains.t: ① The Bull Keeps Running — With a Referee
steps: Where the year stands: S&P +11.89%, Nasdaq +12.47%, Dow +8.20% — one S&P record close added in October (10/6), and the bull turned four on 10/12
The engine: AI capex and earnings — Nvidia still up 14.8% YTD; TSMC posted a sixth straight record quarter
The character: record runs met re-tests, not breaks — dips stayed buyable until the inflation prints landed
The breadth: Energy (+52.6%) leads the year; Comms (-6.3%) now lags
chains.d: The bull holds — four years old — as AI and earnings carry the year; the 10Y, the war and now CPI-PPI tax the rest.

news.fact: Chipmakers, which have soared over 80% so far this year, were clear underperformers on the day, falling 3.4%.

The bull market turned four on Monday, with many strategists expecting more room for stocks to run. However, concerns over an AI bubble, elevated Treasury yields, and geopolitical uncertainty present hurdles.

steps: The rates tax: the 10Y climbed from 4.16% to 5.09% (+93bp; 30Y +59bp) — and fresh 24-year highs were printed into October
The Fed answered: a September hike (first since July 2023); December prices ~89%, October ~17% (22% before CPI, 37% at the peak) — the hot prints round-tripped
The barrel: the war has crude up 76.6% YTD; CPI's gasoline line (+34.2% y/y) is the pass-through — pump prices $4.33/gal vs $3.08 a year ago
The toll: gold -3.7%; rate-sensitives lag and multiples stay capped
chains.d: 2026's second inflation wave: the Fed re-hiked, the 10Y paid +93bp — and this month showed the CPI-PPI channel is still live.

news.fact: Tight global crude supplies during the Iran war have sent US crude soaring more than 60% so far this year, stoking inflation pressures. In response to those pressures, the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in September for the first time since July 2023.
Consumers pay $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, compared to about $3.08 per gallon a year earlier, according to AAA.
'Inflation is alive and the only way the Warsh Fed knows how to kill it is with another dose of higher rates,' said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.

chains.t: ③ The AI Platform — and the Stress Test It Grew Into
steps: The platform: capex keeps compounding — TSMC's record quarter is the proof
The buildout moved onto credit: SpaceX's $40B raise; Broadcom's $50B for OpenAI; CoreWeave's debt — bond yields now above 15%
One revenue scare (FT, 10/8) — answered within a day (Bloomberg, 10/9)
The stress test deepened: an eighth straight chip slide into month-end, a global memory repricing (CXMT), and a credit gauge at a record
chains.d: The AI trade's year: capex compounding, funded on credit — a revenue question answered; then competition, memory and rate stress — deepened into October.

news.fact: A little over a week after it was reported that OpenAI's annualized revenue was approaching $70 billion, the AI lab is said to have told investors the real figure is some $20 billion lower — 'approaching $50 billion.'
Bloomberg reported that OpenAI expects to reach or exceed $70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year, helping quell worries that the AI boom is running out of steam.

Selling has been particularly intense in CoreWeave, which has issued $22 billion of bonds and $26 billion of loans, according to LSEG data. A CoreWeave bond that was issued in June yielding 9.625% recently yielded 15%.
CoreWeave's bonds sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%.

steps: The war's eighth month: crude up over 60% this year — the supply-risk hum under the whole tape
The month's flashpoints: the war's heaviest tanker-attack week; 24 ships hit in the two weeks to 10/11; a container ship sank in Hormuz
The storm layer: Isaias briefly shut in nearly two-thirds of Gulf output
The policy stack: 20M+ barrels of diesel agreed for release this month (G7/IEA) — and a Russia diesel deal now facing legislation
chains.d: War as the norm: the premium lives in the barrel; the offsets live in policy.

news.fact: Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began — cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October; of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers and two others were crude oil tankers.
Approximately 62.9% of daily offshore oil production, or 1.28 million barrels per day, has been shut in as Hurricane Isaias strengthens.

steps: From cuts to hikes: the Fed hiked in September — its first increase since July 2023
The odds: October ~17% (22% before CPI), December ~89% — the hot prints round-tripped
The dollar +3.6% as the regime re-priced; gold down 3.7% — real rates dominated
Ahead: the Oct 27-28 meeting and a December decision the market prices ~89% — every print still bends the whole curve
chains.d: The regime changed in 2026: cuts became hikes, the dollar firmed — and the October prints moved odds 22% → 37% → ~17%, a full round trip.

news.fact: Fed Governor Christopher Waller said additional rate hikes will probably be necessary, but the timing of those hikes is 'flexible.'

According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 29% likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks, and an 88% likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting.
